analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the estate-tax exemption to $4 million per estate, with inflation indexing.
analysis.headline: The estate-tax cut was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, got no cosponsors, and died there without a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the amount of an estate exempt from federal estate and gift taxes to $4 million, up from the $675,000 phase-in level in effect in 2000, and kept raising it with inflation each year [S2][S3]. Only estates large enough to exceed the new $4 million exemption would pay any less, and the tax savings would go to their heirs [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced in September 2000, sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of people leaving estates worth several million dollars. In 2000 the exemption was phased in at $675,000, so the change would have erased estate tax entirely for estates up to $4 million and cut it for larger ones [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the unified estate and gift tax credit so that the first $4 million of an estate is exempt from federal estate tax [S2][S3].
Adjusts the $4 million exemption upward each year after 2001 for cost-of-living increases, so the protected amount grows over time [S3].
Rounds the inflation adjustment to the nearest $10,000 and applies the change to deaths and gifts after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through the revenue the government forgoes on very large estates; the burden of the estate tax falls almost entirely on inheritances over the exemption level, so any lost revenue must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The benefit is concentrated at the very top: with a $4 million exemption, no estate below that size owes any estate tax, so the entire tax cut flows to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates while the revenue loss is borne broadly [S2][S3].

The bill also rewrites the family-owned-business exclusion in Section 2057 to reference the new $4 million amount, which would shrink the extra exclusion available to family-business owners who used that provision — a tradeoff that reduces one estate-tax break for small business owners in order to pay for a larger blanket exemption [S3].
Permanently indexing the exemption to inflation locks in growing revenue losses every year, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes to a narrow group — heirs of estates between roughly $675,000 and $4 million and above — while the cost spreads across all federal taxpayers. It is a straightforward tax cut for large inheritances with no offsetting revenue source, and it even trims the family-business exclusion to help fund it. Whatever one thinks of the estate tax, this bill was designed so its gains flow overwhelmingly to the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2000 and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Moran of Kansas introduced the bill on September 7, 2000 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever receiving a committee vote or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, large estates continued to pay estate tax as under existing law, and the federal Treasury kept that revenue. Wealthy heirs were worse off than they would have been under the bill, and general taxpayers were spared the revenue loss.

for.name: Rep. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the estate-tax exemption to $4 million with inflation indexing.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 7, 2000 and never scheduled it for consideration, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern can be measured [S4][S5].

industries.note: Estates exceeding the old exemption would owe hundreds of thousands of dollars less in federal estate tax, with the largest inheritances gaining the most. The gain comes directly out of federal revenue that other taxpayers must make up.

Every dollar of estate tax forgiven is revenue the government does not collect, which would have to be replaced through other taxes, borrowing, or lower spending. With permanent inflation indexing, the loss would grow each year.
